I need to make a decision in this Monopoly turn.

I have $2166 and a pink monopoly with four houses on each property. The opponent is in jail with $94 and heavily mortgaged holdings. Two other players are bankrupt.

I am reconsidering my strategy of avoiding hotels on the pink properties. The opponent currently has zero houses available, which prevents them from breaking down hotels or building new ones.

Standard Monopoly rules require four houses in the bank to sell a hotel. With zero houses available, I cannot sell a hotel unless I first remove all buildings from the color group.

The opponent cannot sell individual hotels or light-blue houses because the bank has no houses. Even-build rules may also block them from selling houses unevenly.

Even-build rules require selling houses evenly across a color group. A hotel counts as five houses, so the opponent cannot sell houses from four-house properties while a hotel remains on the set. They must first break down the hotel before selling any houses.

The opponent's red properties contain only houses, not hotels. They can sell these back to the bank for $75 each, generating roughly $600 in cash. This gives them about $694 in total liquidity alongside their $94 cash.

Virginia Avenue at four houses costs $700, which would bankrupt the opponent. St. Charles and States at four houses cost $625, leaving them with about $69 after selling all red houses. They have no get-out-of-jail-free cards.

Paying the $50 bail would leave the opponent with $44 cash. Their total liquidity would then be about $644, enough to survive St. Charles or States but not Virginia Avenue.

I am also calculating hotel costs. Each pink hotel likely costs $100, since it replaces four houses at the same price as one house.

Hoteling the pink properties would return twelve houses to the bank. That would let the opponent break down their hotels and liquidate dark blues and light blues.

Selling houses would lower my rent below their liquidation line and also put houses back into the bank for them.

Unmortgaging the Pennsylvania Railroad or Tennessee Avenue is not worthwhile. I lack the other orange properties to complete a monopoly, and the railroad alone is weak.

Trading would give the opponent cash, which helps them survive.

I will not trade Tennessee Avenue to complete the opponent's orange monopoly. I already have the killing pink monopoly, so I do not need more properties. I am considering buying Park Place and Boardwalk from them to eliminate their dark-blue threat.

The opponent will not sell their dark blues cheaply. I am now calculating whether my $2166 cash can cover the cost of buying Boardwalk and Park Place.

I confirmed that Park Place at four houses costs $1300 and Boardwalk at hotel costs $2000. My $2166 cash covers both without needing to buy them.

The previous turn's strategy of ending without building, selling, unmortgaging, or trading remains sound.

Jail is a mixed blessing. It protects the opponent from my pink properties but also keeps them out of reach.

I am now calculating the rent values for the opponent's light-blue properties. Oriental and Vermont at four houses cost $450, while Connecticut at four houses costs $400. These light-blue rents are significant enough to make buying both dark blues worthwhile despite the cash cost.

The dark blues are the only real threat. Connecticut at four houses costs $550, and Oriental or Vermont at four houses costs $450, both easily affordable.

The red properties are harmless right now because the opponent has zero houses in the bank. They cannot build more reds, so keeping the bank frozen is the best weapon.

I am now considering whether a trade could give me something without requiring me to return houses to the bank.

I have decided that trading is not worthwhile. The opponent will not give up their dark-blue properties for mortgaged holdings, and offering cash would only help them survive. I am ending my turn.
